name: omen

attributes.attribute: may read the past as well as the future
for the Celts tied to odd beast or star action
seen through a window, the bad averted with bows
for Scots sailors a sign of a drowning
read death in a hen, a dog, or a gap in a field
its turn told of luck either way

sources: Carmichael, Alexander. Carmina Gadelica: Hymns and Incantations. Hudson, N.Y.: Lindisfarne Press, 1992, pp. 176–178.
Harland, John, and T. T. Wilkinson. Lancashire Legends. (London: George Routledge and Sons, 1873), 228+.
Ross, Anne. Folklore of the Scottish Highlands. London: B. T. Batsford, Ltd., 1976, 94.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: To read an omen is not always to look into the days ahead. The sign may aim at something already met far off, a way of seeing through the bend. Some belief in omens stays in every people, for some folk always seek to know more than their raw senses may tell. The Celts tied omens to odd motion by beasts or to odd signs among the stars, and they did not always part the telling from the causing. A crescent moon glimpsed through a window once brought bad luck, and a triad of bows toward that moon sent the luck away. A rat loose on a ship told Scots sailors that a mate could sink. The Irish named plain death omens: a gap in a field sowed, a hen that cried from its perch, or a dog that wailed three nights running. A horseshoe worked as an oracle, since the closed end facing the finder meant luck at hand, while the shoe turned out spelled ill.

okr.objective: Describe the omen as a mark of fate that looks ahead, falls behind, or reaches to events unseen.
key_results: Scots sailors took a rat on board as a sign a shipmate would drown.
The Irish read death from a howling dog.
The setting of a horseshoe told whether luck went well or ill.
Bows toward a moon glimpsed through a window turned aside the worry.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
